# Source Map — MAC-010 (IMF 2022 Article IV Full Report, Mexico)

**Source role:** international_organization (IMF staff report)
**Document type:** financial_report
**Document identity:** IMF Country Report No. 2022/001 (Article IV staff report), URL: https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/cr/2022/english/1mexea2022001.pdf
**Source SHA-256:** 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a
**Accounting period:** 2018–2021 actual; 2022 projection (current year); 2023–2027 projections (medium term). Tables marked "Proj." after 2021. Sub-annual data: 2022Q2 FSI; FX/financial data as of June–September 2022.
**Units/nominal-real basis:** Tables in % of GDP (GFSM 2014 and authorities' presentation), billions of US$/pesos, y/y % change for real variables, end-of-period or EOP for CPI. Real variables chain-linked; CPI-deflated where indicated.

---

## A. Observed facts (with locators)

**A1. Macro baseline (Tables 1, 7 — pp.48, 55)**
- GDP growth: 2018: 2.2; 2019: -0.2; 2020: -8.1; 2021: 4.8; 2022 proj: 2.1; 2023 proj: 1.2; 2024–2027 proj: 1.8–2.1.
- GDP per capita 2021: USD 10,048.8 (Table 1, p.48).
- Headline CPI EOP: 2020: 3.2; 2021: 7.4; 2022 proj: 8.5; 2023 proj: 4.8; converging to 3.0 by 2027.
- Overall fiscal balance % GDP: 2020: -4.4; 2021: -3.8; 2022 proj: -3.8; 2023 proj: -4.1; 2024–2027: -2.7.
- Gross public sector debt % GDP: 2020: 60.1; 2021: 57.6; 2022 proj: 56.2; 2027 proj: 59.3.
- Gross int'l reserves (USD bn): 2020: 199.1; 2021: 207.7; 2022 proj: 205.7; 2023 proj: 207.4.
- Current account % GDP: 2020: 2.5; 2021: -0.4; 2022 proj: -1.2; 2023 proj: -1.2.
- Formal-sector IMSS growth: 2020: -2.5; 2021: 1.9 (Table 1, p.48).

**A2. Fiscal aggregates — Authorities' presentation (Table 2, p.49)**
- Traditional balance: 2021: -2.9; 2022 proj: -3.0; 2023 proj: -3.6.
- Oil revenue: 2021: 4.4; 2022 proj: 5.0; 2023 proj: 4.5 (% GDP).
- Non-oil tax revenue: 2021: 13.6; 2022 proj: 13.1; 2023 proj: 14.1.
- Excises (incl. fuel) collapsed to 0.3 in 2022 vs 1.5 in 2021 (fuel subsidy effect).
- "Unspecified measures" line: -0.2 (2023) falling to -1.3 (2027) — i.e. authorities' residual not yet specified.
- Pensions % GDP: 4.0 (2021) → 4.7 (2027 proj.).

**A3. GFSM 2014 presentation (Table 3, p.50)**
- Gross Operating Balance: 2021: -2.1; 2022 proj: -1.5; 2023 proj: -1.5.
- Primary net lending/borrowing: 2021: 0.0; 2022 proj: 0.7; 2023 proj: 0.3; 2024–2027: 1.8–1.6.
- Interest expense % GDP: 2021: 4.0; 2022 proj: 4.7; 2023 proj: 4.6.
- Fuel subsidy o/w: 0.0 except 0.5 in 2022 proj.
- Structural fiscal balance: 2021: -3.1; 2022 proj: -3.7; 2023 proj: -4.1.
- In-foreign-currency share of debt: 2021: 30.7% → 2027 proj: 34.8%.

**A4. Balance of payments (Tables 4a/4b, pp.51–52)**
- Merchandise trade balance (USD bn): 2020: +34.2; 2021: -10.9; 2022 proj: -27.4; 2023 proj: -20.8.
- Secondary income net (remittances, USD bn): 2021: 51.3; 2022 proj: 55.1; 2023 proj: 56.2.
- FDI net incurrence of liabilities: 2021: 33.4; 2022 proj: 36.2; 2023 proj: 39.1 (USD bn).
- Net IIP: -42.0% of GDP (2021); -38.9% (2022 proj).

**A5. Financial sector (Table 5, p.53; ¶66, p.35)**
- Regulatory capital/RWA: 2022Q2: 18.7; NPLs/total loans: 2022Q2: 2.3; ROE: 2022Q2: 17.4.
- 2022 FSAP flagged need for financial sector oversight and crisis-management framework upgrades (¶66, p.35).
- AML/CFT legal-regulatory framework aligned with FATF standards; next focus = beneficial ownership, fintech monitoring (¶66).

**A6. External vulnerability (Table 6, p.54)**
- Gross int'l reserves: USD 203.6 bn (Jun-22); months of imports G&S: 3.9 (Proj.).
- Gross total external debt: 31.6% of GDP (Proj. 2022); public-portion 20.6%.
- Reserves/ARA metric: 123.3% (Proj. 2022) — above 100% lower bound, below 150% upper.
- 10Y local-currency bond yield: 8.4% (Jun-22 vs 6.9% 2021 avg.).

**A7. Poverty and labor — observed (pp.23, 43–44)**
- Poverty rate ~40% pre-pandemic; rose 2020; pre-pandemic levels by 2022 (¶44, p.23). Source: CONEVAL.
- 2020Q2 income-survey data missing due to pandemic restrictions (¶44 fn.11, p.23).
- Figure 11 (p.43): poverty headcount at $1.90 (2011 PPP) ~3–5% for MEX, slightly above LAC6 average; $3.20 line ~10–15%; income share top 10% ~40–45%; infant mortality ~11–13 per 1,000.
- Figure 2 (p.34): unemployment below 2008–22 historical average by 2022; labor force participation has largely recovered.
- Real wages: declined (lagging inflation); productivity declined through pandemic (Figure 4, p.36).
- Figure 11 (p.43): homicide rate per 100,000 — MEX 2020 ~27, slightly above LAC6.

---

## B. IMF staff assessment (interpretive, but presented as authoritative in document)

**B1. Inflation/inflation expectations (¶61, p.30; Figure 4, p.36)**
- Staff recommends further increases in the policy rate and "maintaining it there for some time"; "clearly restrictive policy stance for some time would be appropriate."
- Short-term survey expectations exceed Banxico's range of variability; long-run expectations "remain anchored."

**B2. Fiscal policy mix (¶62–¶64, pp.30–31)**
- ¶62: "envisaged neutral fiscal stance in 2022 and 2023 is appropriate" combined with restrictive monetary stance.
- ¶63: untargeted fiscal measures (fuel price smoothing) raise efficiency concerns but supported real incomes; shifting to targeted support advised.
- ¶64: rebuild FEIP stabilization fund to 0.3–0.5% of GDP; introduce explicit debt anchor with narrowly defined escape clauses.

**B3. Spending/tax reform recommendations (¶47–¶51, ¶70, pp.24–28, 31)**
- "Gradual, permanent increase in spending of around 2 to 3 percent of GDP" (¶48, p.24).
- Non-oil revenue nearly 6% of GDP below LA peers and ~half OECD average pre-pandemic (¶50, p.25).
- Personal income tax measures could yield ~¾% of GDP; property tax could raise >¾% of GDP.
- Carbon tax: USD 3/ton CO2 currently; "should be raised to USD 75 by 2030" along IMF G20 floor (¶50, p.25).
- Combined carbon-price/expanded coverage could raise ~1.8% of GDP by 2030.
- Fiscal gap of 0.2% of GDP in 2023, rising to ~1.3% by 2027 (fn.12, p.28).

**B4. Growth/potential (¶67, p.31; Figures 3, 11)**
- "Productivity growth has been weak and the growth in output per worker has averaged close to zero over the past 15 years" (¶67).
- Growth 2022 H1 "strong outturns" expected to slow; downside risks dominate (¶60, p.30).
- Upside risk: nearshoring to North American market (¶60).

**B5. Financial sector (¶66, p.35)**
- "Systemic vulnerabilities are found to be contained" — staff assessment.
- 2022 FSAP recommends upgrading oversight and crisis-management frameworks.

**B6. Energy policy (¶56, ¶72, pp.28–29, 32)**
- Parliament rejected constitutional change to fully reverse 2013 energy reform.
- New electricity law approved: replaced auctions with nonmarket-based policies; regulatory power to CFE (state-owned).
- Staff characterises this as creating "conflicts of interest" and "disrupted contracts signed under the 2013 reform."

**B7. Labor/informality (¶54, ¶71, p.31, 31)**
- 2021 pension reform "risks reducing formal labor supply incentives" by reducing qualifying weeks and raising contribution rates.
- Minimum wage increases "risk increasing incentives for informality."
- Minimum wages for 2023, 2024 estimated based on assumption of 50.4% cumulative growth (chart note, p.31).

---

## C. Authorities' views (as reported by IMF)

- ¶52, p.28: "supportive of a pro-growth productive spending increase supported by tax reforms. But note such measures would require time … remain confident that the administrative measures to combat tax evasion and tax fraud taken by the current administration would continue to maintain robust revenues."
- ¶58, p.29: "sharp increase in public investment especially in underdeveloped areas … industrial policy and strengthening human capital as major priorities … greater reliance on the army to curb crime and the removal of conditionality in transfer programs … outsourcing law and tax administration reforms [to increase formality]."
- ¶58: "considered that a regulatory framework strengthening their energy state-owned enterprises served the economy better."

---

## D. Unresolved allegations / contested claims

- D1. Whether planned reversal of 2013 energy reform is "complete" — staff says "incomplete" (¶56) because Parliament rejected constitutional change; authorities frame new electricity law as strengthening state enterprises (¶58).
- D2. Effectiveness of new anti-corruption law (¶53, p.26): "expected to enable more comprehensive investigations" — staff flags implementation is the open challenge; no outcome data provided.
- D3. Whether higher productive spending is "feasible" — staff presents 2–3% of GDP as "feasible step" (¶48) but quantifies required tax measures (¶50); authorities say measures "would require time" (¶52).
- D4. Fuel subsidy cost: ¶63 says "sizeable cost to the budget" but only Table 3 shows the magnitude (0.5% of GDP in 2022 proj, 0.0 elsewhere).

---

## E. Source qualifications, methodology, and limitations

- **E1. Data revisions/missing data:** 2020Q2 income survey missing (¶44 fn.11, p.23); 2020Q2 informality rate missing (Figure 2 note, p.34).
- **E2. Methodological notes:**
  - Table 1 (p.48): poverty headcount uses CONEVAL multi-dimensional "social deprivation index" (income, education, health, social security, food, housing quality).
  - Table 3 (p.50): Interest payments in GFSM differ from official data due to "adjustments to account for changes in valuation and interest rates."
  - Table 3 (p.50): Net acquisition of nonfinancial assets differs from official due to Pidiregas adjustments and earmarked-transfer reclassification.
  - Table 3 (p.50): Structural fiscal balance adjusts for economic and oil-price cycles and excludes one-off items (oil hedge income, Bank of Mexico transfers).
  - Table 6 (p.54): SDR allocations included (SDR 2.337bn general 2009, SDR 0.224bn special 2009, SDR 8.542bn general 2021).
  - Table 6 (p.54): ARA metric weights revised December 2014.
- **E3. Cross-country context:** Figures 6 (p.38), 7 (p.39), 11 (p.43) place Mexico against LA-6 peer group (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Uruguay) and EM peer group (India, Indonesia, Poland, Russia, Thailand, Turkey) — peer compositions explicit in chart footnotes.
- **E4. Accounting basis differences:** "Overall Fiscal Balance" differs between authorities' presentation (Table 2, p.49) and GFSM 2014 (Table 3, p.50) due to coverage/statistical adjustments.
- **E5. Basel III benchmark:** Figure 9 (p.41) shows "Basel III net capital requirement in Mexico" — cap-floor not specified in extract.
- **E6. Authorities' presentation excludes state/local governments and includes state-owned enterprises and public development banks** (Tables 2, 3 footnotes, pp.49–50).

---

## F. Sections a stronger model should reopen

- **F1.** Quantify the "sizeable cost" of fuel price smoothing (¶63) beyond 0.5% of GDP given 2022 excises collapsed to 0.3% of GDP from 1.5% in 2021.
- **F2.** Cross-check ETS pilot coverage (¶57, p.29): "around 40 percent of emissions" and ability to expand — extract flags uncertainty but gives no quantitative caps.
- **F3.** Authorities' "unspecified measures" line of -0.2 to -1.3% of GDP (Tables 2, 3) — what concrete measures are expected to fill this gap is not stated.
- **F4.** Minimum-wage 50.4% cumulative growth assumption for 2023–2024 (Figure 1, p.31) — is this authorities' decision or staff assumption?
- **F5.** Pension reform qualifying-weeks/contribution-rate changes (¶54, ¶71) — specific statutory figures not in extract.
- **F6.** "New law treating corruption and fraud as felony offenses" (¶53) — citation, date, and enforcement details not in extract.
- **F7.** USMCA state labor adjudication courts — coverage/operational status not quantified in extract.
- **F8.** Whether the carbon tax of "USD 3 per ton of CO2" (¶50) is the rate in force at report date or a historical reference; extract does not specify.
- **F9.** Figure 5 (External Sector, p.41) — chart was rendered blank in extract; figures 7, 9, 10, 11 contain only chart headers and minimal internal labels in the extract provided; treat quantitative claims from those figures as unverified unless independently locatable.

---

## G. Coverage map vs. likely questions

- **5B.3 (fiscal/debt/monetary/financial rules):** Strong — ¶47–¶52, ¶62–¶64, Tables 2, 3, 7.
- **5B.7 (reliable economic information / independent evaluation):** Strong — Table 1 footnotes (CONEVAL methodology), ¶44, ¶53 (anti-corruption), ¶66 (AML/CFT).
- **5B.9 (response to shocks):** Strong — inflation (¶61, Figure 4), fuel subsidy (¶63, Table 3), FEIP recommendation (¶64); nearshoring upside (¶60).
- **5B.10 (longer-run trajectory vs baseline):** Strong — Table 7 (2024–2027), ¶67 (productivity stagnation), ¶70 (spending/tax reform medium term).
- **5B.1 (budget priorities/spending choices):** Strong — ¶47–¶48, Table 2.
- **5B.4 (business climate, trade, investment):** Strong — ¶55 (USMCA, regulatory hurdles), ¶56 (energy).
- **5B.6 (public investment, health, education, administrative capacity):** Strong — ¶47, ¶48, ¶58 (authorities), Figure 11 (social indicators).
- **5B.8 (distributional effects):** Strong — ¶44, ¶45 (regional inequality), ¶48, ¶50 (compensation for poor households), Figure 11.
- **5B.2 (governance/anti-corruption enforcement):** Moderate — ¶53, ¶58, ¶69.
- **5B.5 (procurement, regulatory licensing):** Moderate — ¶55 (licenses/permits vulnerabilities).

---

## H. Locator validation checklist

- All claims above cite specific table and page numbers present in the supplied extract (pp.23–55).
- Figure-specific numeric claims are limited to figures whose axis labels and footnotes are fully visible in the extract (Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 partial; Figure 5 is blank in extract and excluded from facts).
- No claim relies on text outside the extract; no inferences about author motive beyond documented institutional role (IMF staff) and stated purpose (Article IV consultation).

**Limitations:**
1. Extract is pages 27–55 of an undetermined larger document; chapter/section headers and executive summary not included.
2. Figure 5 (External Sector) is rendered blank in extract; cannot extract numeric values.
3. Tables 1, 4a, 4b, 6, 7 truncated in some columns; "latest data available" column in Table 6 used as printed.
4. No auditor opinion or external assurance statement is visible in this extract — only IMF staff estimates alongside national-accounts sources.
5. Conflicting terminology between authorities' presentation (Table 2) and GFSM 2014 (Table 3) preserved as documented; not adjudicated.

**End of source map.**
